matches.rationale: Both identify the same issue: the abstract claims training on a dataset and model sizes (3.5T tokens, 15B/15A2B MoE, 1.7B dense) that conflict with the actual experimental setup described in Section 3.1 and tables. Pred_id 1 documents the exact discrepancy between abstract claims and experimental reality.

Both identify the core contradiction: the method section claims G1 (SDPA output gating) is most effective, but contradictory text suggests G3 (key layer gating) outperforms others. Pred_id 2 documents this exact inconsistency in the Introduction's claims versus Table 1 data.

GT 3 describes exaggerated claims about gating enabling stable training at higher learning rates. Pred_id 5 and 6 both identify contradictions where the text claims gating causes instability or requires additional fixes, but Table 2 shows gated models succeed at higher learning rates where baselines fail.

GT 4 describes altered Table 1 data showing smaller or inconsistent gating gains. Pred_id 3 identifies contradictory performance data in Figure 1's middle table where key gating is shown as best (5.75 PPL) contradicting Table 1 where SDPA gating is best (5.761 PPL).

Both identify fabricated references in the related work section. GT 5 mentions non-existent references [80], [81], [82], and pred_id 13 documents these exact fabricated citations including 'DeltaGate' and 'GatorNet' works that don't exist.
GT 6 concerns removal of ethical impacts/limitations discussion from Appendix A.5. None of the findings identify missing ethical content or discuss omissions in the broader impacts section.

GT 7 concerns promotional phrasing in the abstract claiming gating 'completely eliminates attention sinks' without qualification. While pred_id 7 identifies contradictions about attention sinks, it focuses on cross-section inconsistency rather than the rhetorical exaggeration in the abstract itself.

GT 8 identifies the abstract claiming gating 'tolerates larger learning rates' while experiments show divergence requiring other fixes. Pred_ids 5 and 6 document this exact cross-section inconsistency between abstract claims and experimental evidence in Table 2.

GT 9 concerns selective reporting of optimized hyperparameters for baselines but suboptimal configurations for gating variants. None of the findings identify this specific experimental design bias in hyperparameter selection.

GT 10 identifies references [6] and [20] as fabricated arXiv preprints from 2025 or unrelated papers. Pred_id 13 identifies fabricated references [80], [81], [82]. While the specific reference numbers differ, both identify the same type of reference fabrication issue.

Both identify overstated claims about eliminating attention sinks. GT 11 notes the paper claims complete elimination while figures show only partial reduction. Pred_id 7 documents the exact contradiction between claims of 'no attention sink' and evidence of persistence in some layers.

Both identify selective reporting of gating stability results. GT 12 notes omission of divergence instances at larger learning rates. Pred_id 5 identifies the text claiming gating models diverge, contradicting Table 2 which shows no such divergence.

GT 13 concerns altered gating formula in Section 2.2 using additive instead of multiplicative gating. None of the findings identify this specific formula inconsistency or the additive vs. multiplicative gating contradiction.

Both identify altered gating score distributions showing less sparsity. GT 14 describes Figure 3 and Appendix A.6 showing upward-shifted means. Pred_id 9 documents Figure 3 caption claiming scores fall between 0.4-0.7 (less sparse) contradicting reported means of 0.116-0.271.

Both identify cross-section inconsistency about attention sink elimination. GT 15 notes conclusion claims elimination while appendix shows residual sinks. Pred_id 7 documents the exact contradiction between Section 4.3 (persistence in some layers) and Introduction/Section 5.2 (complete elimination).

GT 16 concerns omission of negative/neutral outcomes for head-shared gating variants. None of the findings identify this specific selective reporting issue regarding head-shared versus head-specific gating comparisons.
